name: Banôho
confidence_why: The only description of stress is Adams's 1907 missionary sketch (repeated almost verbatim in his Anthropos article of the same year), which puts the accent on the penult by default and always on the root syllable of the base form, while the two modern first-hand phonologies of the same Banɔ'ɔ dialect, Kouankem 2003 and Den Besten 2016, describe a two-tone (H/L) system and say nothing about stress, so the morphological reading stands unopposed but rests on a single 1907 account whose 'Ton' may partly reflect tone.
catalog_citation: Adams, P. Gust. Alf. 1907. Die Sprache der Banôho. Mitteilungen des Seminars für Orientalische Sprachen zu Berlin, Jahrgang X, Dritte Abteilung: Afrikanische Studien, 34-83. Berlin: Georg Reimer.

catalog_quote: III. Wortton. Der Ton ruht für gewöhnlich auf der vorletzten Silbe. Bei zusammengesetzten Formen kann er bis auf die drittletzte Silbe beibehalten werden. Wörter, welche nur infolge des Präfixes (Vorsilbe) zweisilbig sind, behalten den Ton naturgemäß auf ihrer Stammsilbe; z. B. diké Ei; dibé Euter, weibliche Brust. Die Grundregel für die Wortbetonung ist also: die Wurzelsilbe der Grundform bleibt immer die starke, kräftige Silbe des Wortgebildes, auch neben einem anderen sekundären Akzent.

new_statements.quote: III. Wortton. Der Ton ruht für gewöhnlich auf der vorletzten Silbe. Bei zusammengesetzten Formen kann er bis auf die drittletzte Silbe beibehalten werden. Wörter, welche nur infolge des Präfixes (Vorsilbe) zweisilbig sind, behalten den Ton naturgemäß auf ihrer Stammsilbe; z. B. diké Ei; dibé Euter, weibliche Brust. Die Grundregel für die Wortbetonung ist also: die Wurzelsilbe der Grundform bleibt immer die starke, kräftige Silbe des Wortgebildes, auch neben einem anderen sekundären Akzent.
new_statements.translation: III. Word stress. The stress ordinarily rests on the penultimate syllable. In compound (complex) forms it can be retained as far back as the antepenultimate syllable. Words which are disyllabic only because of the prefix naturally keep the stress on their stem syllable, e.g. diké 'egg', dibé 'udder, female breast'. The basic rule of word stress is therefore: the root syllable of the base form always remains the strong, forceful syllable of the word, even alongside another, secondary accent.
new_statements.citation: Adams, P. Gust. Alf. 1907. Die Sprache der Banôho. Mitteilungen des Seminars für Orientalische Sprachen zu Berlin, Jahrgang X, Abt. III: Afrikanische Studien, pp. 34-83.
new_statements.locator: p. 37, 'Grammatik. Lautbezeichnung und Aussprache', section 'III. Wortton' (archive.org item bub_gb_vBLgAAAAMAAJ, leaf 670)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: opened the saved page scan (MSOS Jahrgang X, Abt. III, p. 37, running head 'ADAMS: Die Sprache der Banôho'). Under 'Grammatik. Lautbezeichnung und Aussprache', section 'III. Wortton' reads exactly as quoted: 'Der Ton ruht für gewöhnlich auf der vorletzten Silbe. Bei zusammengesetzten Formen kann er bis auf die drittletzte Silbe beibehalten werden. Wörter, welche nur infolge des Präfixes (Vorsilbe) zweisilbig sind, behalten den Ton naturgemäß auf ihrer Stammsilbe; z. B. diké Ei; dibé Euter, weibliche Brust. Die Grundregel für die Wortbetonung ist also: die Wurzelsilbe der Grundform bleibt immer die starke, kräftige Silbe des Wortgebildes, auch neben einem anderen sekundären Akze…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the root (stem-initial) syllable: with the usual prefix + CVCV stem this is the penult; in prefix + CV words it is the final (stem) syllable; when suffixes/extensions are added the stress stays on the root syllable, so it may surface on the antepenult.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mentions that the root syllable stays strongest 'even alongside another, secondary accent' in longer derived forms; no rule for placing the secondary accent is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Prefix+monosyllabic-stem nouns (diké, dibé) stressed on the final syllable; complex verb forms may carry stress on the antepenult. Adams also uses an acute mark on vowels that are 'short, closed and stressed' (p.37, I. Vokale), so his accent marks partly encode vowel quality.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement about citation forms in a 1907 missionary grammar of the Banôho (Banɔ'ɔ/Nohu, A32a) dialect, written before tone was recognised; the modern phonology (Den Besten 2016) analyses Banɔ'ɔ as a two-tone (H/L) language with lexical tone contrasts and says nothing about stress, so Adams's 'Ton/Betonung' may partly reflect stem-initial prominence/high tone rather than stress in the modern sense.
new_statements.identity_note: Adams 1907 describes the Banôho dialect (= Banɔ'ɔ / Bano'o / Nohu, Guthrie A32a) of Batanga as spoken around Kribi; Den Besten 2016 and Kouankem 2003 describe the same Banɔ'ɔ dialect. Glottolog bata1285 (ISO bnm) has no dialect-level glottocodes; the Bapuku/Puku (A32b) and Tanga dialects are not covered by the quoted statement. Not to be confused with the 'Batanga' dialects of Oroko or Caka.

new_statements.quote: Der Ton ruht für gewöhnlich auf der vorletzten Silbe. Bei zusammengesetzten Formen kann er bis zur drittletzten Silbe beibehalten werden. Grundregel ist: die Wurzelsilbe bleibt die starke des Wortgebildes auch neben anderem sekundären Akzent.
new_statements.translation: The accent ordinarily rests on the penultimate syllable. In compound forms it can be kept as far back as the antepenultimate syllable. The basic rule is: the root syllable remains the strong one of the word-form, even beside other, secondary accent.
new_statements.citation: Adams, P. G. A. 1907. Die Banôho und Bapuku in Kamerun. Anthropos 2: 1022-1028.
new_statements.locator: p. 1024, section 'II. Sprachliches', subsection 'A. Lautbezeichnung', last paragraph (archive.org item anthroposephemer2190unse, leaf 1236)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: lines 88362-88365 contain 'Der Ton ruht für gewöhnlich auf der vorletzten Silbe. Bei zusammen¬gesetzten Formen kann er bis zur drittletzten Silbe beibehalten werden. Grundregel ist : die Wurzelsilbe bleibt die starke des Wortgebildes auch neben anderem sekundären Akzent.' and the page scan header '1024 / P. G. A. Adams,', section 'II. Sprachliches', 'A. Lautbezeichnung', last paragraph) shows the passage verbatim, with 'To n' letterspaced for emphasis; maps leaf 1236 -> pageNumber '1024'. I read the whole article (lines 88225-89070): title 'Die Banôho und Bapuku in Kamerun', opening says it compares the Bapuku dialect with the Banôho grammar of MSOS X (1907) Abt. III; the rest (nouns, verbs…
new_statements.relation_note: Same rule, in nearly the same words, as the MSOS X (1907) p. 37 'III. Wortton' statement already recorded for this language (existing_statements); it adds explicitly that the rule holds for both the Banôho and the Bapuku dialect (the article is a comparison of the two). The catalog record for Banôho has an empty rule field; this source supports filling it as penult-by-default / root-syllable-governed. No tone is mentioned; Adams treats the language as having word accent ('Ton', 'Akzent') only, which contradicts nothing in the catalog but differs from later work (Den Besten 2016, Kouankem 2003, both already held by the project) that describes lexical H/L tone and says nothing about stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent normally falls on the penult; in compound (morphologically complex) forms it may stay on the antepenult; the governing principle is that the root syllable is always the strong syllable of the word regardless of affixation, so surface penult placement is a consequence of the mostly disyllabic root plus final vowel, not a positional rule. Adams also notes (same page, 'A. Lautbezeichnung', first paragraph) that unstressed final syllables and particles are heavily reduced in speech ('bis zur betonten Silbe zu verstümmeln, indem unbetonte Endsilben.. unterdrückt werden') and that unstressed u and o become w before a stressed vowel.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mentioned only in passing: the root syllable stays strong 'auch neben anderem sekundären Akzent' (even beside other secondary accent); no placement rule for secondary accent is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Compound forms may keep the accent on the antepenult (the root syllable) rather than the penult.
new_statements.identity_note: Adams 1907 (Anthropos) explicitly covers two closely related dialects, Banôho (the catalog's variety) and Bapuku, and gives the accent rule for both without distinction; the Bapuku forms are given as belonging to the same language ('trotz der großen Verwandtschaft ihrer Dialekte'). Schadeberg 1980 labels the language 'noho A.32' and draws its data from Adams' MSOS grammar. Tupper et al. 2024 is a survey of Batanga (A32) as a whole (Banoo/Bapuku/Batanga varieties) but was not opened.

readall_conflicts: Schadeberg 1980 is silent; Tupper et al. 2024 could not be opened. The standing tension in the file is between Adams (1907, word accent only, no tone) and the later phonological descriptions already held by the project from the 09-17 check (Den Besten 2016 MA thesis, Kouankem 2003), which describe two contrastive tones H/L and say nothing about stress; the two descriptions are not directly contradictory (neither denies the other), but the catalog's stress reading rests on a 1907 missionary description that may have been hearing tone as accent.

sources.note: Acoustic questionnaire study of stem-initial accent in seven NW Bantu languages incl. Bapuku; states that Bapuku is the only sampled language WITHOUT stem-initial accent and that it has penultimate vowel length instead. This bears on the word-prosody (accent) side rather than the tone inventory; tone is mentioned only for Eton (accented syllables host two tones).

tone.quote: In order to evaluate the hypothesis that the stem-initial accent in NW Bantu is realised only or mainly through consonant length, we recorded questionnaires for seven NW Bantu languages (Bapuku, Basaa, Eton, Fang, Kota, Kwasio, Bagyeli) ... The only language in our sample that lacks stem-initial accent is Bapuku, which has penultimate vowel length and which lacks the typical NW Bantu morphosyntactic characteristics.
